title: William Calk’s 1775 journal
summary: On March 13, 1775, William Calk set out from Prince William County, Virginia, for Kentucky, keeping a daily journal of the trip until May 2.
bodyMarkdown:
On Monday, March 13, 1775, William Calk set out from Prince William County, Virginia, for the Kentucky country. He kept a daily journal of the trip until May 2. The original is part of the Calk Family Collection at the Kentucky Historical Society, which describes it on its [digital collections page for the journal](https://www.kyhistory.com/digital/collection/Calk2/id/6/).

## A land venture

KHS calls the trip "a great land speculation." Calk's party may have been drawn by Richard Henderson's advertisements for a new colony. Henderson's [Transylvania Company](https://grokipedia.com/page/Transylvania_Colony) did not claim title until March 17, 1775, when it signed its purchase agreement with Cherokee leaders at Sycamore Shoals. The deal bypassed the Proclamation of 1763, which banned private purchases of Native land west of the mountains.

Calk traveled with Abraham Hanks, the grandfather of Abraham Lincoln, along with Philip Drake, Enoch Smith and Robert Whitledge. Several enslaved people also made the journey. The KHS record notes that their names were not written down.

## On the road

The party crossed the Blue Ridge to the Powell River Valley. On April 4 they joined Henderson's company near Cumberland Gap. Henderson had already sent Daniel Boone and a crew of axmen ahead on March 10 to clear a trail, the route later known as the [Wilderness Road](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wilderness_Road).

Boone's party reached the Kentucky River on April 1 and soon met armed resistance from Native people in the area. News of the fighting frightened many travelers on the road behind them. Hanks and Drake turned back for Virginia.

Calk pushed on. He reached "Boons foart" on Thursday, April 20, 1775. After drawing a lot, he and his two remaining companions built a house and planted corn to secure their claim.

## A voice from the frontier

KHS notes that Calk's journal "has been called the most colorful account to survive from the period." It is full of personal comments and everyday trouble. The University of North Carolina also holds a [typescript copy of the journal](https://finding-aids.lib.unc.edu/catalog/00131), covering March 13 to May 2, 1775.

The broader Calk Collection includes land and business papers kept by several generations of the family.

## Later life

Calk (1740–1823) worked as a surveyor, merchant and land speculator. He lived first at [Boonesborough](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boonesborough,_Kentucky), then built a cabin and later a house near Hinkston Creek in present-day [Mount Sterling](/stories/mount-sterling-little-mountain-town/). In 1804 he took a boat loaded with corn, tobacco, bacon and lard down the rivers to New Orleans. He recorded that trip in a second journal, also now at KHS.

## Kentucky today

The Kentucky Historical Society keeps the 1775 journal in Frankfort and has put page images and a transcription online. Its plain record of mud, fear and land claims remains one of the best-known settler accounts from Kentucky's first season of organized migration.
